intros.market: The WebPKI certificate market remains highly concentrated, with the top 3 CAs controlling 74% of issuance and the top 5 reaching 91%. Internet Security Research Group (Let's Encrypt) leads at 36.2%, followed by Google Trust Services at 21.2% and DigiCert at 16.7%. The market HHI of 2208 indicates moderate concentration, while 75 of the 89 trusted CAs operate in the long tail with minimal issuance volume.
intros.trust: Browser root stores show significant disagreement, with 335 total roots distributed unevenly across four trust stores and only 90 roots trusted by all four programs. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating operational complexity where certificate chains trusted in Edge may fail validation in other browsers. Only 38 CA owners appear in all four stores, forcing certificate authorities to maintain multiple hierarchies and complicating chain-building logic for relying parties.
intros.conc: The ecosystem exhibits dangerous systemic dependency, with the top three CAs responsible for nearly three-quarters of all certificates protecting the web. An operational failure at Internet Security Research Group alone would impact more than one-third of HTTPS connections globally. The HHI of 2208 sits well above competitive market thresholds, and the 91% share held by just five organizations means that distrust events at any major CA create widespread disruption, as the distrust history demonstrates.
intros.tail: Seventy-five certificate authorities hold full trust store inclusion despite issuing a negligible fraction of certificates, creating asymmetric risk where low-volume CAs carry the same browser trust as high-volume operators. These tail CAs collectively represent the majority of trusted entities but contribute minimally to web coverage, yet each retains the technical capability to issue for any domain. The incident data shows 54 CAs have been involved in security events, many of them tail operators lacking the operational maturity of high-volume issuers.
intros.geo: United States-based CAs dominate global issuance at 92.57% despite representing only 15 of 89 trusted authorities, while Europe hosts 44 CAs but accounts for just 7.33% of certificates. Asia-Pacific's 17 CAs issue only 0.1% of certificates, and the Americas and Middle East/Africa regions combined represent 9 CAs with effectively zero market share. This extreme geographic concentration means that US regulatory decisions, legal frameworks, and operational practices disproportionately shape global WebPKI security posture.
intros.gov: Thirty state-operated or state-owned certificate authorities maintain trusted roots despite issuing only 0.08% of certificates, creating the same asymmetric risk profile seen in the commercial long tail. These government CAs are distributed across multiple regions and subject to sovereign jurisdiction pressures detailed in the jurisdiction risk analysis. Their presence in trust stores gives nation-states the technical capability to issue certificates for any domain, regardless of actual issuance volume or operational transparency.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high risk for compelled disclosure or state access to CA operations: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk under current legal frameworks. These classifications intersect with geographic concentration data showing that while most issuance originates in the United States, trusted roots span 89 CAs across all regions, many operating under legal regimes that permit or require cooperation with intelligence services.
intros.ops: The ecosystem has recorded 1,587 incidents across 54 CAs, with misissuance (614 events) and governance failures (510) representing the dominant categories. Self-detection accounts for only 27% of discoveries, while external researchers find 18% and automated tools 16%, indicating that CAs frequently fail to identify their own operational failures. Policy violations (199) and disclosure failures (139) demonstrate that many incidents stem not from technical complexity but from basic compliance breakdowns, with root program oversight catching only 4% of issues.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture varies widely across the 335 roots in browser trust stores, with legacy RSA key sizes and aging signature algorithms still present alongside modern profiles. Certificate authorities must navigate overlapping and sometimes conflicting cryptographic requirements across four root programs, each with different deprecation timelines for algorithms and key sizes. The distrust history shows that weak cryptographic posture correlates with broader operational immaturity, though the digest does not provide granular algorithm distribution data for this measurement period.
intros.distrust: Browsers have executed 16 formal distrust actions, with 14 of those events attributed to compliance and operational failures rather than technical compromise. Seven cases involved negligent noncompliance, three demonstrated incompetence, and three rose to willful circumvention of requirements, while only one was classified as accidental. The median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement spans 1,185 days, and 10 of 16 events followed a pattern of repeated issues rather than isolated incidents, indicating systemic CA operational failures.
intros.policy: Of 36 active TLS issuers measured, only 8 have achieved the 47-day certificate validity posture required by March 2029, while 5 remain at risk of missing the March 2027 100-day threshold and 3 have not yet reached the March 2026 200-day requirement. The compliance challenge extends beyond validity periods: the regulatory surface has grown 121x since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations across baseline requirements, root program policies, and audit standards, with 76% classified as mandatory. CAs face an expanding rule set with zero new ballots since 2022 to rationalize the accumulated complexity, making operational readiness increasingly difficult even for well-resourced issuers.
intros.governance: Root program oversight participation has collapsed, with Chrome responding substantively to only 18.4% of the 223 incidents in 2025, down from 67.8% in 2019, while Mozilla fell from 78.0% to 9.9% and Apple from unmeasured to 5.4%. Microsoft provides zero substantive oversight despite maintaining 142 exclusive roots not trusted by other browsers. Chrome has participated in 732 oversight bugs with 293 substantive responses, and Mozilla in 818 bugs with 249 substantive responses, but recent engagement has declined sharply even as the incident rate remains high.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum has 56 members, but only 21 actively contribute while 35 maintain zero participation in ballot proposals or endorsements. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo leads individual participation with 36 ballots proposed and 1 endorsed, while Sectigo as an organization ranks as the top contributor overall. This silent majority pattern means a small group shapes policies binding on all trusted CAs, and the regulatory surface data shows zero ballots since 2022 even as complexity has grown to 6,657 obligations, suggesting governance stagnation despite operational pressure.
intros.audit: Annual audit letters detected only 31% of incidents that occurred during their examination periods, meaning clean audit opinions routinely coexist with real operational failures documented in Bugzilla. Of 80 parsed audit letters covering 83 CAs, 39 show high transparency gaps between audit scope and actual incident history, and 4 contain qualified opinions signaling material control deficiencies. WebTrust self-reporting reaches 59.4% while ETSI reaches 66.9%, but auditor concentration remains moderate at HHI 541.4, with KPMG covering 11 CAs and the top five auditors covering 35 CAs combined, and 11 CAs changed auditors in 2025.
